Welcome toOort's Turning Galaxy

Nearby stars all circle the Galactic centre as fast as the Sun: do any approach or recede?

About: differential rotation of the Galactic disc seen from the Sun, and the first Oort constant A

About this simulation

On screen
The disc face-on, turning clockwise, drawn to scale: the Galactic centre with small x and y axes at the top, the Sun 8.2 kpc below it on the dashed arc of its orbit with its velocity v0 to the left, a 1 kpc scale bar, and a ring of 36 stars at distance d coloured red when receding and blue when approaching (grey below 0.5 km/s). The probe draws the line of sight at longitude l, the line s to the centre, a dotted piece of that point's orbit and its velocity vc(s). The inset plots each ring star's vr against its current longitude.
Controls
The rotation curve (flat, Keplerian or rigid, all 230 km/s at the Sun) and the ring distance d, 0.5 to 2 kpc, re-form the ring at t = 0. The probe longitude l, 0° to 360°, moves only the probe. Play runs the rotation to 20 Myr in about 10 s and then re-forms the ring; ⏮ Rewind to t = 0 re-forms it at once.
Measured
Every vr is the exact vr = [ω(s) − ω0] s0 sin l, positive receding; the ring stars are carried forward exactly in the frame turning with the Sun, so the centre stays at the top and the Sun stays still. From question 5 on, the Readouts panel also shows Oort's constant A = ½[v0/s0 − (dvc/ds)0] and the first-order value A d sin 2l at the probe.
Assumptions
Every star, the Sun included, moves on an exact circular orbit in a thin disc, with s0 = 8.2 kpc and v0 = 230 km/s. The Sun's own motion relative to the circular orbit (about 20 km/s) and the random motions of real stars are left out, so real radial velocities scatter about these values. vr ≈ A d sin 2l is only first order in d/s0; the probe readout vr is exact.

Guided Inquiry

1 · Ring stars seen from the Sun

Choose the flat rotation curve, set the ring distance to d = 1 kpc and leave the rotation at 0 Myr. Every star on the ring moves round the centre at 230 km s−1, the same speed as the Sun. Before looking at the colours of the ring, predict the radial velocities of the ring stars relative to the Sun.

2 · The probe at 45 degrees

Keep the flat curve and d = 1 kpc, and set the probe longitude to l = 45°, a direction between the centre and the direction of the Sun's motion. Before reading the probe, predict the radial velocity of the star there.

3 · Letting the ring turn

Keep the flat curve and d = 1 kpc; the ring starts again at t = 0. Before pressing play and letting the rotation run to 20 Myr, predict how the ring changes in the view that turns with the Sun.

4 · A ring twice as far

The ring starts again at t = 0. Keep the flat curve and the probe at l = 45°, and change the ring distance from d = 1 kpc to d = 2 kpc. Before moving the slider, predict what happens to the radial velocity at the probe.

5 · A Keplerian curve

Set d = 1 kpc again, keep l = 45°, and switch from the flat curve to the Keplerian curve, in which the circular speed falls as s−1/2 but still equals 230 km s−1 at the Sun. Before switching, predict the radial velocity at the probe.

6 · Rigid rotation

Keep d = 1 kpc and l = 45°, and switch to rigid rotation, in which vc ∝ s and the Sun still moves at 230 km s−1. Before switching and pressing play, predict what the ring does.

7 · What you found

Seen from the Sun, nearby stars in a disc that turns differentially have vr ≈ A d sin 2l: four arcs round the sky, receding towards l = 45° and 225°, approaching towards 135° and 315°.

Oort's constant A = ½[v0/s0 − (dvc/ds)0] measures the shear, not the rotation: 14.0 km s−1 kpc−1 for a flat curve, 21.0 for a Keplerian one and 0 for rigid rotation (see the Readouts). Measured values are about 15 km s−1 kpc−1, close to the flat curve.

Nearby Stars in a Turning Galaxy

✦Learn this with the AI tutor

01

At a glance

Stars of the Galactic disc all circle the centre, and the Sun is one of them. This sim looks down on the disc, puts a ring of stars at distance d around the Sun, and shows each star's radial velocity as seen from the Sun, for three different rotation curves.

What you'll learn

  • What sets a star's radial velocity seen from the Sun.
  • How it depends on longitude l and distance d.
  • How the rotation curve enters, through Oort's constant A.
  • What happens to a ring of stars as the disc turns.
The set-up, face-on. The centre lies far above the top of the figure.

What's on screen

  • Orange dots: the Galactic centre (top, with small x and y axes) and the Sun, 8.2 kpc below it on the dashed orbit, with its velocity v0 to the left. The disc turns clockwise.
  • Ring of 36 stars at distance d from the Sun, coloured red when receding and blue when approaching, grey when |vr| < 0.5 km/s.
  • Probe: the circled star and its line of sight at longitude l.
  • Inset: vr of every ring star against its longitude, with the probe marked by a vertical line.
See itLook at the opening scene. Watch for: the Sun at the middle of the ring, and the circled probe star on its line of sight at l = 45°.

03

A difference in angular speed sets the radial velocity

A star at longitude l and distance d from the Sun lies at distance s from the centre and moves on a circle at its circular speed vc(s). Its angular speed is ω(s) = vc(s)/s, and the Sun's is ω0 = v0/s0 = 28.05 km s⁻¹ kpc⁻¹. Subtracting the Sun's velocity and keeping the part along the line of sight gives, in the notes (7.5):

vr = [ ω(s) − ω0 ] s0 sin l
The geometry of the notes' Fig. 86, with d drawn much larger than in the sim. Positive vr means receding.

So vr depends on angular speeds, not on circular speeds. On the flat curve vc = v0 at every radius, so ω(s) = v0/s. A star nearer the centre than the Sun has the larger ω and pulls ahead of it; a star further out falls behind.

For l = 45° and d = 1 kpc the star is at s = 7.53 kpc, so ω = 30.56 km s⁻¹ kpc⁻¹ and vr = (30.56 − 28.05) × 8.2 × sin 45° = +14.6 km/s.

Key idea. Equal circular speeds are not equal angular speeds: vr measures ω(s) − ω0.
See itLook at the probe on the flat curve, at d = 1 kpc and l = 45°. Watch for: the probe's vr reading +14.6 km/s in the Readouts panel.
04

Four arcs round the ring: vr follows sin 2l

For stars near the Sun (d ≪ s0) the notes expand to first order: s ≈ s0 − d cos l, so ω(s) − ω0 ≈ −(dω/ds)0 d cos l. With 2 sin l cos l = sin 2l (notes 7.8, 7.9):

vr ≈ A d sin 2l, A = −½ s0 (dω/ds)0

The wave has two lobes above zero and two below. Stars towards l = 45° and 225° recede, those towards 135° and 315° approach, and at d = 1 kpc on the flat curve the extremes are about ±14 km/s. The size scales with d.

Flat curve, d = 1 kpc. Solid: the sim's exact vr. Dashed: A d sin 2l with A = 14.0 km s⁻¹ kpc⁻¹.

A d sin 2l is only first order in d/s0; the sim's vr is exact. At l = 45° they read 14.6 and 14.0 km/s, and from d = 1 to 2 kpc the exact value rises from 14.6 to 29.8 km/s, a factor 2.04 where the first-order formula says 2. At l = 90° it gives zero, the exact value is −1.7 km/s.

See itTurn the probe to l = 135° on the flat curve at d = 1 kpc. Watch for: the probe star turning blue and vr reading −13.4 km/s.
See itNow set d = 2 kpc, with the probe back at l = 45°. Watch for: vr rising from 14.6 to 29.8 km/s.
05

The ring stretches into an ellipse as the disc turns

The view turns with the Sun, so the Sun and the centre stay put while each star moves round at ω(s) − ω0 relative to the Sun. Stars nearer the centre move ahead, those further out fall behind, so the ring cannot keep its shape.

There is a simple reason for the ellipse. The radial velocity vr is the rate at which a star's distance from the Sun changes, and 1 km/s is about 1.02 pc per Myr. Receding stars move outwards and approaching stars move inwards: over 20 Myr, a star receding at 14.6 km/s gains about 0.3 kpc.

Flat curve, d = 1 kpc, in the view that turns with the Sun. Dashed: the ring at t = 0. Dots: the same stars at t = 20 Myr.

After 20 Myr, about a tenth of the Sun's 219 Myr period, the d = 1 kpc ring on the flat curve is roughly an ellipse. Its far stars lie about 1.3 kpc out, near l = 50° and 235°, and its near stars about 0.75 kpc out, near 140° and 325°. The long axis lies close to the 45° to 225° line.

See itPress Play on the flat curve at d = 1 kpc. Watch for: the dashed starting circle staying put while the ring stretches into an ellipse as t climbs to 20 Myr.
06

The rotation curve sets A: flat, Keplerian or rigid

A is set by how fast the angular speed falls with radius. In terms of the circular speed (notes 7.11):

A = ½ [ v0/s0 − (dvc/ds)0 ]

The sim's three curves share v0 = 230 km/s and differ only in the slope (dvc/ds)0: 0 for flat, −v0/2s0 for Keplerian, +v0/s0 for rigid.

curveA (km s⁻¹ kpc⁻¹)vr at 1 kpc, 45°: exact / first order
flat14.014.6 / 14.0 km/s
Keplerian21.022.3 / 21.0 km/s
rigid00 / 0 km/s

On the rigid curve ω = ω0 at every radius: no star gains on the Sun, and vr = 0 all round the ring, although the circular speeds differ. vr measures the shear in the rotation, not the rotation itself.

curve d l

07

Where it matters

  • Measuring the Galaxy's rotation. Radial velocities of stars at a given distance vary as sin 2l, and the amplitude divided by d gives A; proper motions give the second Oort constant B = A − ω0. This is how Oort showed in 1927 that the Galaxy rotates differentially.
  • The measured values in the notes are A ≈ 15 and B ≈ −12 km s⁻¹ kpc⁻¹, so ω0 = A − B ≈ 27 km s⁻¹ kpc⁻¹. Then (dvc/ds)0 = −(A + B) is small: near the Sun the real rotation curve is close to flat. A flat curve with the sim's v0 and s0 would give A = 14.0 and B = −14.0, so it is close but not exactly flat. The sim does not show B.
  • Real stars scatter. The sim leaves out the Sun's own motion (about 20 km/s) relative to a circular orbit and the random motions of stars, so measured radial velocities scatter about the sin 2l pattern.
08

Summary

In one line. Seen from the Sun, a star's radial velocity depends on the angular speeds of the disc, and so it reveals how the disc's rotation changes with radius.

Key points

  • vr = [ω(s) − ω0] s0 sin l, with ω = vc/s.
  • For d ≪ s0, vr ≈ A d sin 2l: four arcs, receding towards 45° and 225°.
  • A = ½ [v0/s0 − (dvc/ds)0]: 14.0, 21.0 and 0 km s⁻¹ kpc⁻¹ for the flat, Keplerian and rigid curves.
  • The turning ring shears into an ellipse, because vr is the rate of change of each star's distance.

Common mix-ups

  • "Equal circular speeds mean no radial velocity." Equal speeds are not equal angular speeds: the flat-curve probe at 45° recedes at 14.6 km/s.
  • "Doubling the distance exactly doubles vr." Only the first-order formula does; exactly it is a little more.
  • "Rigid rotation is the case with the most shear." It has none: A = 0 and every vr is zero.

Things to try on your own

  • On the flat curve set l = 90° and compare vr with the first-order value.
  • Play the rotation at d = 1 kpc and at 2 kpc and compare the stretching.
  • Put the probe at l = 135° and cycle through the three curves.
